assets.title: The next decision should win the screen
assets.subtitle: An appointment screen, before and after. Hypothetical example.

slides.title: Same capability. Different priority.
body: The customer came to choose a time. Put that decision before the full calendar.

annotations.label: Hierarchy
annotations.detail: The next available time answers the immediate question.

annotations.label: Context
annotations.detail: Duration and team appear before the commitment.

annotations.label: Trade-off
annotations.detail: The weekly overview moves behind the booking decision.

assets.caption:
A product's point of view is visible in the decision it makes easiest. You can often see it before reading a line of brand copy.

In this hypothetical appointment screen, both versions offer the same capability. One opens with a calendar to interpret. The other starts with an available time, gives enough context to choose it, then keeps the full calendar within reach.

I'd review the hierarchy against the customer's task before discussing visual references. The useful argument is whether choosing a time deserves the first screen, and what someone loses when the calendar becomes secondary.

assets.title: A promise is a product decision
assets.subtitle: Trace a claim through the first useful task.

slides.title: Put the claim next to the actual task.
body: Keep the exact claim. Rewriting it during the review hides the disagreement.
Hypothetical product: a reporting tool promising a report in minutes.

panels.label: Customer promise
panels.title: A report in minutes
panels.body: The website creates an expectation before the customer knows how setup works.

panels.label: First useful task
panels.title: Create a report from a file
panels.body: The customer needs a result they can inspect before choosing whether to continue.

slides.title: Trace the expectation through the experience.
body: Read each step from the customer's side. Look for the point where the promise stops being believable.

nodes.label: Promise
nodes.title: A report in minutes
nodes.detail: Expectation: I can try this now.

nodes.label: Setup
nodes.title: Wait for approval
nodes.detail: A requirement the claim did not explain.

nodes.label: Result
nodes.title: Open the first report
nodes.detail: The result arrives after a different process.

slides.title: Separate a copy gap from a capability gap.
body: The same complaint can require a different response. Diagnose the missing condition before choosing the work.

rows: Approval is required, but never disclosed.
Approval is unnecessary for a sample report.
A path to try the product.
All reports need a manual review.

slides.title: Compare the decisions, including their cost.
body: A narrower claim can be the right decision. A faster path can be the right decision. Each needs a reason.

panels.label: Change the promise
panels.title: State the approval step
panels.body: Less product work. The customer can decide whether the process suits them.

panels.label: Change the experience
panels.title: Let a sample run immediately
panels.body: More product work. Check data limits and support cost before offering it.

slides.title: Check the expectation before the click.
body: Show the revised claim and give the first task. Ask what the person expects to happen next.
Then watch the task. Record the moment their expectation differs from the product.

nodes.label: Before
nodes.title: Expected result
nodes.detail: What do they think they will get, and when?

nodes.label: During
nodes.title: Observed attempt
nodes.detail: Where do they hesitate or seek an explanation?

nodes.label: After
nodes.title: Account of the result
nodes.detail: Can they explain the requirement in their own words?

slides.title: Write a decision someone can act on.
body: Example decision: allow a sample report before approval. Keep approval for connecting a live account.
Review the claim again when the required setup changes.

fields.label: Change and boundary
fields.hint: What will change? What will remain a requirement?

fields.label: Evidence to inspect
fields.hint: Which customer expectation and task attempt should we observe?

fields.label: Owner and review point
fields.hint: Who can make the change, and when will we inspect it?

assets.caption:
A claim such as 'a report in minutes' creates a product requirement. The team then has to decide what counts as a report, when the clock starts and which prerequisites the customer should know about.

This carousel follows a hypothetical reporting tool from the website to its first result. An undisclosed approval step is the point where the claim and the experience separate. There are several possible responses, including a narrower promise or a sample the customer can try immediately.

If a product decision is holding your early-stage team back, describe the problem in the comments. I am building my consulting practice and would welcome a relevant conversation.

assets.title: Should this be a redesign?
assets.subtitle: A decision worksheet with a completed example and review criteria.

slides.title: Start with the task, then state the proposed change.
body: Hypothetical example: a customer is comparing subscription plans. The proposal is to redesign the pricing page.
Keep the task specific enough to try. A broad goal such as improve conversion cannot explain which decision failed.

fields.label: Customer and situation
fields.hint: Who is choosing, and what brings them to this screen?

fields.label: Task and current proposal
fields.hint: What should they finish? What change has been proposed?

panels.label: Completed example
panels.title: Compare two plans
panels.body: A customer needs to find whether both plans include the feature they came for.

slides.title: Record an observation without turning it into a cause.
body: An observation describes what happened. The explanation remains an interpretation until it has support.

rows: The person opens both plan pages to find export limits.
The comparison does not explain the difference.
The plan names may also be unclear.
The person returns to pricing after reaching checkout.
They may be checking the billing period.
A founder dislikes the card style.
This says nothing yet about the customer task.

slides.title: Write down the evidence you can inspect.
body: Separate the record from your explanation. A preference can be recorded honestly without being presented as customer evidence.

fields.label: Observed action or words
fields.hint: What happened? Keep the wording or sequence as recorded.

fields.label: Source and context
fields.hint: Where did it happen, when, and during which task?

fields.label: Limit of the record
fields.hint: What does this observation leave unknown?

slides.title: Choose the size of the response.
body: Compare a local change with a wider redesign. Write the dependency each introduces.

panels.label: Local change
panels.title: Put export limits in the comparison
panels.body: Keeps the structure. Requires a reliable source for each plan limit.

panels.label: Wider change
panels.title: Rebuild the plan comparison
panels.body: May help several difficult comparisons. Requires evidence across those decisions.

slides.title: Compare your own two responses.
body: Use the completed pricing example as a guide. Give the smaller response a fair comparison with the proposed redesign.

fields.label: Local response
fields.hint: Which specific obstruction would this change address?

fields.label: Wider response
fields.hint: Which repeated cause would justify a larger change?

fields.label: Dependency and cost
fields.hint: What needs to be settled, and what work does each response introduce?

slides.title: Use a rubric, not a vote on the mockup.
body: These are decision criteria, not a score with a scientific cutoff. An unresolved critical dependency can outweigh several benefits.

rows: Can a person find the relevant plan difference?
Does the same issue recur in other key comparisons?
Consider wider work when the cause repeats.
Are plan rules settled and available?
Resolve uncertain rules before presenting them.
Can the smaller change be tested and withdrawn?
Use it to learn when the cost is low.

slides.title: Plan a check that can change your mind.
body: Give someone a plan-selection task without naming the feature location. Compare how they find and explain the relevant difference.

fields.label: Question and task
fields.hint: What decision is difficult? What will the person try?

fields.label: Observation to record
fields.hint: Where do they look? What do they believe is included?

fields.label: Reason to revise
fields.hint: What result would make us reject our preferred response?

slides.title: Keep the decision and its limits together.
body: Example decision: add export limits to the comparison before commissioning a full page redesign.
A successful task attempt supports this local change. It does not establish an effect on revenue.

fields.label: Selected change and rationale
fields.hint: Name the response and the evidence behind it.

fields.label: Uncertainty and boundary
fields.hint: What remains unknown? Which conclusion can we not make?

fields.label: Owner and review date
fields.hint: Who will check the revised task, and when?

assets.caption:
A redesign request often combines a customer getting stuck, an unresolved product rule and a preference about the visual direction. I want those recorded separately before the team approves a larger piece of work.

This worksheet uses a hypothetical pricing-page example. It shows how to record an observation, keep the explanation open, compare a local fix with a wider redesign and choose a test that could change the decision.

The downloadable version has room for your own evidence and includes a review rubric. Use it in the approval meeting. If the observation is missing, the next useful piece of work is to find out what happens during the task.

assets.title: A problem brief you can challenge
assets.subtitle: Separate the observation, explanation and proposed response.

slides.title: Name the difficult decision.
body: Hypothetical example: an operations lead is assigning a request to a team. They need to know who can accept it now.

fields.label: Person and situation
fields.hint: Who is making the decision, and what changed?

fields.label: Current obstruction
fields.hint: Which information or step prevents the person from finishing?

slides.title: Keep evidence and explanation in separate columns.
body: A workaround can reveal a missing piece of information. It does not yet tell you which interface should provide it.

rows: The lead messages team owners before assigning a request.
The product does not show current capacity.
Does capacity change too quickly to publish?
The lead keeps a separate team list.
Team ownership is hard to find.
Does the list contain rules the product lacks?

slides.title: Record the observed event.
body: A useful record names the situation and action before adding the team's explanation.

fields.label: Event and action
fields.hint: What did the person actually do?

fields.label: Source and date
fields.hint: Where can someone inspect the evidence?

fields.label: Missing information
fields.hint: What do we still need to learn about this event?

slides.title: Set boundaries that protect the decision.
body: A useful boundary tells the designer which assumptions are settled and which can still be challenged.

panels.label: Within this work
panels.title: Assignment and team availability
panels.body: Review the information a lead uses to choose a team.

panels.label: Outside this work
panels.title: Changing staffing policy
panels.body: Record the dependency if the assignment problem cannot be solved without it.

slides.title: Write the constraints and dependencies.
body: A boundary should explain why it exists, so the team knows when another discussion is necessary.

fields.label: Fixed constraint
fields.hint: Which rule or condition must the work respect?

fields.label: Open choice
fields.hint: Which decision can this work still change?

fields.label: Dependency owner
fields.hint: Who can resolve a condition outside this work?

slides.title: Write a brief someone can disagree with.
body: Example brief: help a lead see which team can accept this type of request before assignment.
Open question: can availability be maintained accurately enough to support the decision?

fields.label: Problem statement
fields.hint: Describe the person, task and observed obstruction.

fields.label: Alternative cause
fields.hint: What else might explain the same observation?

fields.label: First check
fields.hint: What would distinguish the two explanations?

slides.title: Agree the test and next commitment.
body: Choose a check that could make the team revise its preferred explanation.

fields.label: Next check
fields.hint: What can we observe or compare?

fields.label: Decision condition
fields.hint: Which result would favour a different explanation?

fields.label: Owner and review point
fields.hint: Who will inspect the evidence before choosing the response?

assets.caption:
A problem statement becomes useful when someone can challenge it. 'Make assignment easier' leaves room for almost any proposal. 'Show which team can accept this request before assignment' exposes a dependency the team needs to discuss.

This worksheet uses a hypothetical operations example to separate evidence from the current explanation. The workaround is real only when you have observed it. The proposed cause still needs checking.

Fill in the brief with product, engineering and the people doing the task. If you disagree on the cause, write down the observation that would help settle it before choosing a screen.

assets.title: An empty state is a first-use decision
assets.subtitle: An invoicing screen before and after.

slides.title: Explain the result before asking for work.
body: Explain the result before asking for work.

screens.label: After
screens.title: Track unpaid invoices
rows: Track payment after creating an invoice.
You need a customer and an amount.

annotations.label: Purpose
annotations.detail: Payment status explains why this view exists.

annotations.label: Effort
annotations.detail: The required information appears before the action.

annotations.label: Control
annotations.detail: A draft makes it clear that creation does not immediately send.

assets.caption:
An empty state asks the customer to do work before the product has shown much of its value. The copy needs to make that effort understandable.

In this hypothetical invoicing screen, 'Get started' leaves several questions open. What am I creating? What will I need? Will it be sent immediately? The revised screen answers those questions before the click and explains what the view will show afterward.

I'd test this without an introduction from the team. If the person can explain the next action and what it will do, the empty state is doing its job.

assets.title: Ask for the event, then follow the decisions
assets.subtitle: Interview questions that leave room for a different explanation.

slides.title: Start with a recent occurrence.
body: Use a specific task. Give the person time to recall what happened before asking for their opinion.

panels.label: Prediction
panels.title: Would you use a team dashboard?
panels.body: The answer may describe an intention or respond to the idea you just introduced.

panels.label: Recall
panels.title: Tell me about the last time you assigned a request.
panels.body: A recent event gives you actions, information and decisions to ask about.

slides.title: Follow the information, not your feature.
body: When they mention a tool or message, ask what they needed from it. Keep the proposed solution out of the question.

nodes.label: Trigger
nodes.title: What started the task?
nodes.detail: Find the situation and the information needed.

nodes.label: Decision
nodes.title: What did you try next?
nodes.detail: Follow the action and the workaround.

nodes.label: Result
nodes.title: How did you know it was done?
nodes.detail: Find the actual completion condition.

slides.title: Replace questions that announce the answer.
body: A follow-up should help the person explain the event. It should not recruit agreement for a design.

rows: What were you looking for on this screen?
How did you find out that the request had changed?
How did you decide which requests to open?
Would you pay for this feature?
What do you use now, and what does that cost you?

slides.title: Keep the finding narrower than the story.
body: Hypothetical finding: the lead asks a teammate for current capacity before assignment.
Possible explanations include missing visibility, unreliable data or a rule that needs human judgement.

fields.label: Observed behaviour
fields.hint: Record the action and the context.

fields.label: Competing explanations
fields.hint: Write at least one plausible alternative cause.

fields.label: Next check
fields.hint: What could distinguish those explanations?

assets.caption:
A customer can give a thoughtful answer to a hypothetical feature and still tell you very little about the task. I want the recent event first: what started it, what information they needed, what they tried and how they knew it was done.

These slides show how to move from a leading question to a question about that event. They also keep the conclusion open. A person messaging a teammate might need better visibility, but they might also be dealing with unreliable information or a decision that cannot be reduced to a status.

The interview is useful when it gives you a better question to test. Treating the first plausible explanation as a feature brief skips that work.

assets.title: Define the first complete task
assets.subtitle: A release boundary that includes failure, recovery and deliberate omissions.

slides.title: Choose a task with an observable finish.
body: Hypothetical booking release: a customer chooses a time and receives a confirmed appointment.
A selected slot without a confirmed booking is an incomplete task.

nodes.label: Entry
nodes.title: Find an available time
nodes.detail: Customer can understand which times are offered.

nodes.label: Commitment
nodes.title: Choose and confirm
nodes.detail: Required details and conditions are visible.

nodes.label: Completion
nodes.title: Receive confirmation
nodes.detail: The booking exists and the customer can find it again.

slides.title: Record the task and recovery paths.
body: Write the necessary paths before choosing the screens. Use the booking example to check what the task needs when something fails.

fields.label: Entry condition
fields.hint: What does the customer have or know when the task begins?

fields.label: Completion
fields.hint: What result can they inspect to confirm the task is finished?

fields.label: Recovery
fields.hint: What can they do when the expected path fails?

slides.title: Include the paths needed to trust the task.
body: A smaller release can still need an error path. Decide what the customer can do when the happy path fails.

rows: Keep entered details and offer another time.
A waitlist if not needed for the chosen task.
Show the confirmed booking in the product.

slides.title: List the rules the release depends on.
body: Unsettled rules can change the task more than another interface iteration.

fields.label: Rule or data source
fields.hint: What must be accurate for the task to work?

fields.label: Owner and readiness
fields.hint: Who can confirm it is usable for this release?

fields.label: Fallback
fields.hint: What will the customer see if it is unavailable?

slides.title: Make omissions explicit.
body: An omission needs a reason and a condition for reconsideration. Otherwise it can return as an argument in every review.

fields.label: Capability left out
fields.hint: What are we choosing not to include?

fields.label: Reason and risk
fields.hint: Why can the chosen task work without it? Who is affected?

fields.label: Review condition
fields.hint: What observation would make us add it?

slides.title: Check the boundary with the whole task.
body: Walk entry, confirmation and recovery together. Confirm the team knows which part proves the release is usable.

fields.label: Task and completion condition
fields.hint: Write what the person should be able to finish.

fields.label: Critical dependency
fields.hint: Which data, policy or service must be reliable?

fields.label: Release evidence
fields.hint: What will we inspect before calling this ready?

assets.caption:
A first release can have a short feature list and still leave the customer's task unfinished. Choosing a time matters less if the booking never becomes clear or recoverable.

This worksheet draws the boundary around one hypothetical booking task, including the paths for an unavailable time, a lost slot and a missing confirmation message. It asks which capabilities can wait and why.

I'd review that boundary with engineering before estimating individual screens. The difficult discussion is usually the dependency or failure path the feature list left out.

assets.title: Where does the promise become believable?
assets.subtitle: Trace the claim to the first result a customer can inspect.

slides.title: Keep the proof inside the first task.
body: Hypothetical reporting product: the customer should see a usable sample before deciding whether to connect a live account.

nodes.label: Promise
nodes.title: See your data clearly
nodes.detail: The claim raises an expectation about understanding.

nodes.label: Proof
nodes.title: Open and inspect a sample report
nodes.detail: Find a figure and its source before connecting an account.

nodes.label: Next commitment
nodes.title: Connect a live account
nodes.detail: Ask for access after showing what it enables.

annotations.label: Review question
annotations.detail: If the first task proves something else, revise the path or narrow the claim.

assets.caption:
A customer should be able to inspect the promised benefit before making the next large commitment. That is a useful way to review onboarding.

For a hypothetical reporting product, a sample can show whether the report is understandable before the customer connects a live account. The sample still needs to behave like the product. A polished screenshot with no source or interaction would answer a different question.

I'd trace the promise to the first result someone can examine, then check what the product asks them to commit before that moment.

assets.title: A design review needs a decision boundary
assets.subtitle: Separate the evidence, recommendation and unresolved choice.

slides.title: State what this meeting can decide.
body: Example review: choose how a customer compares two subscription plans.
Pricing policy has already been approved. Plan names are still open for discussion.

panels.label: Open decision
panels.title: Comparison structure
panels.body: The review can change how differences are presented.

panels.label: Fixed constraint
panels.title: Approved plan rules
panels.body: A different price needs another owner and a separate decision.

slides.title: Show the evidence before the proposal.
body: Use the observed task and the condition behind the recommendation. A screen tour alone gives the room little basis for feedback.

nodes.label: Task and evidence
nodes.title: Choose the plan with export
nodes.detail: They open both plan pages to find the relevant limit.

nodes.label: Proposal
nodes.title: Put limits side by side
nodes.detail: Explain which gap the change addresses.

nodes.label: Review question
nodes.title: Is the comparison sufficient?
nodes.detail: Keep the discussion on the open choice.

slides.title: Sort feedback by what it changes.
body: Do not make evidence and preference compete as if they were the same kind of comment. Both can matter, for different reasons.

rows: A customer cannot find the export limit.
Legal needs the renewal condition visible.
Discuss hierarchy and the intended direction.
Find evidence before changing the default.

slides.title: Record the decision and the dissent.
body: A dissenting view is useful when it names a risk the next test can inspect. Keep it beside the decision.

fields.label: Decision and reason
fields.hint: Which option did we choose, and why?

fields.label: Unresolved risk
fields.hint: Which objection still needs evidence?

fields.label: Owner and next check
fields.hint: Who will resolve it before the next commitment?

assets.caption:
A review is easier to lead when the room knows which decision is open. If the pricing policy is fixed but the comparison structure can change, say that before showing the screen.

This agenda puts the customer task, the observation and the recommendation in order. It gives different kinds of feedback a place to go instead of allowing a visual preference, a legal constraint and a new market assumption to become one undifferentiated list.

Leave the review with a decision and the important dissent beside it. The next check should address the risk you still believe could make the decision wrong.

assets.title: Give the first designer authority that matches the job
assets.subtitle: A founder worksheet for scope, ownership and the first real problem.

slides.title: Choose the immediate mandate.
body: A first designer can cover several disciplines. The mandate still needs a priority when those disciplines compete for time.

panels.label: Mandate A
panels.title: Make the core task usable
panels.body: Spend early time on product decisions, research access and shipping with engineering.

panels.label: Mandate B
panels.title: Establish the market-facing direction
panels.body: Spend early time on positioning, identity and the product moments that must support the claim.

slides.title: Set the mandate for the current stage.
body: Write the immediate priority and what should wait when responsibilities compete.

fields.label: Immediate mandate
fields.hint: Which kind of decision needs the most help now?

fields.label: Secondary responsibilities
fields.hint: What else is expected, and at what priority?

fields.label: Work deliberately deferred
fields.hint: What should the designer not be judged on yet?

slides.title: Write the decision rights.
body: Being responsible for the experience means little when every decision can be reopened without a clear owner.

rows: Recommend and resolve within agreed constraints.
Shape and challenge with customer evidence.
Explain the customer cost of each option.

slides.title: Agree the working relationship.
body: A title does not explain how the founder, product lead, engineer and designer will make decisions together.

fields.label: Daily partners
fields.hint: Who brings product context and engineering constraints?

fields.label: Escalation
fields.hint: Who resolves a disagreement the working team cannot settle?

fields.label: Customer contact
fields.hint: How will the designer hear from the people using the product?

slides.title: Describe the first problem honestly.
body: Give candidates the current task, the evidence you have and the access they will get. Avoid a disguised request to fix everything.

fields.label: Current problem
fields.hint: Which customer decision or business claim is unclear?

fields.label: Available evidence and access
fields.hint: What can they inspect? Who can they speak to?

fields.label: First decision to make
fields.hint: Which choice should their work help the team make?

slides.title: Check the role before writing the advertisement.
body: If the designer owns a result but cannot reach customers or influence priorities, the role needs another discussion.

fields.label: Responsibility and authority
fields.hint: Which outcomes are expected? Which decisions can they affect?

fields.label: Support and constraints
fields.hint: Who is the working partner? What cannot change?

fields.label: Evidence of a useful start
fields.hint: What should be clearer after the first problem is investigated?

assets.caption:
The first designer's job can stretch from product flows to a pitch deck in the same week. The hiring brief should explain which responsibility wins when both need attention.

This worksheet puts the mandate and decision rights ahead of the tool list. It also asks what the designer can inspect, who they can speak to and which early problem the team actually wants them to understand.

I am interested in founding designer roles where product decisions and brand direction need to be built together. A clear conversation about authority and access tells me more about that opportunity than a long list of deliverables.

assets.title: Read the decision behind the portfolio
assets.subtitle: A review lens for ownership, alternatives and the limits of the result.

slides.title: Choose one consequential decision.
body: Ask for a choice that changed the direction of the work. Leave time to discuss the option the team did not choose.

nodes.label: Situation
nodes.title: What needed deciding?
nodes.detail: Task, constraint, stakes and plausible alternatives.

nodes.label: Choice
nodes.title: Why this response?
nodes.detail: State the evidence and judgement used.

nodes.label: Afterward
nodes.title: What did you learn?
nodes.detail: Include the result and its limits.

slides.title: Separate authorship from team output.
body: Specific credit makes the reasoning easier to assess. Collaboration should not have to disappear to make a case study sound strong.

rows: A specific contribution and its effect.
A reason grounded in later evidence.

slides.title: Check whether the result supports the claim.
body: A shipped screen proves the team shipped a screen. A task test and a business outcome answer different questions.

panels.label: Supported claim
panels.title: People could locate the plan limit in the test
panels.body: State the task, test conditions and remaining uncertainty.

panels.label: Unsupported extension
panels.title: The new comparison increased revenue
panels.body: Requires separate evidence that can support that conclusion.

slides.title: Leave room for judgement under uncertainty.
body: A good answer may explain why the team acted with incomplete evidence, how it limited the risk and what it planned to check next.

fields.label: Decision worth examining
fields.hint: What did they choose, and what did it affect?

fields.label: Evidence and limits
fields.hint: What could the team know at the time?

fields.label: Next question
fields.hint: What would you need to understand their judgement?

assets.caption:
A polished case study can hide the part I most want to understand: the choice that was difficult before the final screen existed.

I'd ask the designer to reconstruct that decision. Which alternatives were plausible? Which constraint mattered? What did they own? What did someone else contribute? Then I would check whether the stated result supports the claim being made.

The aim is to understand their judgement, including the moments when the team had to act before all the evidence was available. Honest boundaries make that conversation more credible.

assets.title: Classify the cost before cleaning it up
assets.subtitle: Choose the response by the cost of leaving it.

slides.title: Use the consequence to choose the response.
body: Name who pays the cost before choosing the work.

rows: Plan limits are hard to compare.
Inspect the task; show the missing information.
Teams rebuild the same input behaviour.
Agree the behaviour; reuse a component.
A setting uses a different button style.
A status has two different meanings.
Settle the rule before standardising it.

annotations.label: Priority check
annotations.detail: Who pays the cost now, how often does it occur, and what would delay make worse?

assets.caption:
A cleanup list can put a confusing plan comparison beside a mismatched button as if they have the same consequence. That makes prioritisation harder than it needs to be.

I would classify the cost first. A customer struggling to make a decision needs evidence about the task. Repeated implementation work may need a shared behaviour. A visual difference needs an explanation of whether it is intentional. An unresolved product rule needs an owner before it gets a component.

This matrix gives each issue a first response. The priority still comes from the people affected, the frequency and the cost of leaving it in place.

assets.title: Write the brief around a decision
assets.subtitle: A working agreement for evidence, constraints and approval.

slides.title: State the decision the work should help make.
body: Hypothetical brief: decide how a customer can compare plans before reaching checkout.
A deliverable such as redesign pricing is useful only after the difficult decision is clear.

fields.label: Customer task
fields.hint: What should the customer understand or finish?

fields.label: Current obstruction
fields.hint: Which part of the task is difficult today?

slides.title: Record the evidence and the competing explanation.
body: Keep a customer observation separate from the founder's diagnosis so the work can test both.

fields.label: Observed evidence
fields.hint: What happened during the task?

fields.label: Current explanation
fields.hint: Why do we think it happened?

fields.label: Alternative to inspect
fields.hint: What else could explain the same behaviour?

slides.title: Give the designer the rules and the unknowns.
body: Keep settled decisions separate from assumptions. Otherwise exploration can accidentally reopen a constraint or harden an untested belief.

rows: Treat as a constraint unless an owner changes it.
Customers choose mainly by export needs.
Legal wording is still under review.
Name the owner and review point.

slides.title: Put the omissions in the agreement.
body: Example boundary: review comparison and checkout information. Do not revise the pricing policy in this work.

fields.label: Included work
fields.hint: Which part of the task will we examine?

fields.label: Deliberate omission
fields.hint: What related work is excluded, and why?

fields.label: Reason to change scope
fields.hint: What evidence would require another discussion?

slides.title: Agree access and approval.
body: Customer access, product data and decision ownership determine what the designer can responsibly conclude.

fields.label: Evidence and access
fields.hint: Which task recordings, customer conversations or product data are available?

fields.label: Decision owner
fields.hint: Who approves the choice? Who advises or constrains it?

fields.label: Review point
fields.hint: When will the team inspect the evidence and make the decision?

slides.title: Define a useful handoff.
body: State what the team needs to understand and use after the work. A file alone may not carry the rules behind the decision.

fields.label: Decision record
fields.hint: What choice and reasoning should travel with the work?

fields.label: Rules and edge cases
fields.hint: Which conditions must the implementation preserve?

fields.label: Review after release
fields.hint: Who will inspect the task once the change is in use?

assets.caption:
A founder's design brief should help the designer make a sensible choice when the founder is not in the room. That requires more than a list of screens.

This worksheet records the customer task, the decision the work should help make, the settled rules and the assumptions still open for challenge. It also asks who can approve the choice and which evidence the designer can access.

Use it as a working agreement. If customer access or approval is unclear, settle that before treating a delivery date as the main constraint.

assets.title: Trust depends on what the customer can verify
assets.subtitle: Review permission, price, failure and recovery at the moment of commitment.

slides.title: Explain access before requesting it.
body: Hypothetical reporting tool: describe actual access before asking for it.

screens.label: Clearer request
screens.title: Read account data for your report
rows: You can remove access in settings.

annotations.label: Review condition
annotations.detail: Use only permission statements that match the actual integration.

slides.title: Show the commitment where the decision happens.
body: A condition is harder to evaluate when the product reveals it after the customer has invested effort.

rows: Price, billing period and meaningful limits.
When billing begins and how to stop it.
What changes now and what happens to existing work.
What access the person will receive.

slides.title: Make failure understandable and recoverable.
body: A failure message should tell the person whether their work is safe and which action is available now.

panels.label: Unclear
panels.title: Something went wrong
panels.body: The customer cannot tell whether the action happened or whether retrying is safe.

panels.label: Specific
panels.title: The upload failed. Your draft is saved.
panels.body: Offer a retry when it is safe, and explain how to inspect the saved work.

slides.title: Test the expectation, then the behaviour.
body: Before the action, ask what the person believes will happen. After it, ask what they can confirm.

fields.label: Expected commitment
fields.hint: What does the customer think they are agreeing to?

fields.label: Actual behaviour
fields.hint: What will the product really do?

fields.label: Verification and recovery
fields.hint: How can they confirm the result or undo the action?

assets.caption:
Trust is difficult to review as a visual quality. It becomes more concrete when you inspect what the customer can verify before a commitment.

A permission request should describe the actual access. A price should explain the billing condition. A failed action should tell the person whether their work is safe and whether retrying could create a duplicate.

These slides review those moments individually. I'd compare the customer's expectation with the product's actual behaviour, then check whether the result and the recovery path are visible.

assets.title: Judge the decision after the time saved
assets.subtitle: Compare the same task, including review and repair.

slides.title: Keep the task and the review criteria constant.
body: Count review and correction when comparing effort.

rows: Can the flow support the chosen task? Can the team explain its choices?
Which facts or rules were added without evidence?
What must a designer or engineer repair before use?
Draft, review, correction and handoff time.

annotations.label: Boundary
annotations.detail: One comparison informs this task. It cannot establish quality across every kind of design work.

assets.caption:
I would measure the work after the first draft as carefully as the time it took to produce it. A design that arrives quickly can still require a long review if it introduces rules, facts or interaction details nobody agreed to.

This comparison keeps the customer task and review criteria constant. It records task fit, unsupported assumptions, correction effort and whether the team can explain the choices. The total includes the handoff.

That gives a team a useful basis for choosing where a tool belongs in its process. It also keeps one successful trial from becoming a broad claim about every design task.

assets.title: Build only what the question requires
assets.subtitle: A prototype plan for decisions, realism and the limits of a test.

slides.title: Name the decision before choosing fidelity.
body: Hypothetical question: can a person compare plan limits before selecting a subscription?

panels.label: Needed realism
panels.title: Plan names, limits and comparison behaviour
panels.body: These details determine what the person can understand and do.

panels.label: Unnecessary polish
panels.title: Final illustration and account settings
panels.body: Leave these rough when they cannot change the answer to this question.

slides.title: Choose the prototype by what could go wrong.
body: A static view can answer some questions. An interaction question needs enough behaviour to expose the difficult moment.

rows: The comparison states and navigation must work.

slides.title: Plan the necessary realism.
body: Keep the parts that can affect the answer accurate. Record rough areas so observers do not overinterpret them.

fields.label: Must behave accurately
fields.hint: Which interaction or content can change the observation?

fields.label: Can remain rough
fields.hint: Which detail is outside this question?

fields.label: Known prototype limit
fields.hint: What difficulty could come from the prototype itself?

slides.title: Write the task without explaining the interface.
body: Example task: choose a plan that supports the export you need. Do not tell the person which table or button contains the answer.

fields.label: Task to give the person
fields.hint: Describe the goal, not the interface instructions.

fields.label: Observation to record
fields.hint: What choice, hesitation or misunderstanding matters?

fields.label: Help to withhold
fields.hint: Which explanation would hide the difficulty we need to inspect?

slides.title: Agree what would change the choice.
body: Make the evidence condition clear before watching the session.

fields.label: Decision under review
fields.hint: Which option is the team considering?

fields.label: Reason to revise
fields.hint: Which observation would make us reject that option?

fields.label: Decision owner and next step
fields.hint: Who will use the finding, and for which commitment?

slides.title: State what the test cannot establish.
body: A person completing this task can inform the comparison design. It cannot prove what they would buy or how revenue would change.

fields.label: Supported conclusion
fields.hint: Which decision can this observation inform?

fields.label: Remaining uncertainty
fields.hint: Which question needs a different method or setting?

fields.label: Next commitment
fields.hint: What are we willing to change based on this evidence?

assets.caption:
I choose prototype fidelity by asking which detail could change the answer to the question. For a plan comparison, the names, limits and interaction may need to be accurate. Final illustration may not.

This worksheet connects the decision, the realism required and the task the person will try. It also asks which explanation the moderator should withhold so the test can expose a difficult step.

Write the limit of the conclusion before the session. Watching someone find the right plan can support an interface decision without telling you what they will buy in the real situation.

assets.title: Follow one task across the company
assets.subtitle: A review of the information that changes between marketing, product and support.

slides.title: Trace the same promise through each handoff.
body: Hypothetical task: a customer wants to replace a reporting process with a new tool.

nodes.label: Before signup
nodes.title: What can I expect and commit to?
nodes.detail: Inspect the claim, access, cost and setup requirements.

nodes.label: Inside the product
nodes.title: What do I do next?
nodes.detail: Follow the first report and its explanation.

nodes.label: When it fails
nodes.title: What context must I repeat?
nodes.detail: Inspect support access and ownership of the unresolved task.

slides.title: Look for lost context and conflicting rules.
body: A handoff problem may live in policy, data or ownership. A new screen can only help when that cause is understood.

rows: The setup requirement appears after signup.
Where should the condition be stated?
Support asks for information already provided.
The website and product describe different limits.
The customer is sent between teams.
Who owns the whole unresolved task?

slides.title: Choose the smallest complete response.
body: A complete response covers the customer question through the handoff. Changing one message may leave the cause in place.

panels.label: Message change
panels.title: Clarify the setup requirement
panels.body: Useful when the process is deliberate and the information is missing.

panels.label: Operational change
panels.title: Give support the necessary context
panels.body: Useful when the customer must repeat work because teams cannot see it.

slides.title: Give the gap a shared owner.
body: The review should leave one person accountable for coordinating the response, even if several teams contribute.

fields.label: Customer task and gap
fields.hint: Where does the explanation or ownership break?

fields.label: Cause and proposed response
fields.hint: Which information, rule or process needs to change?

fields.label: Owner and inspection point
fields.hint: Who will review the whole task after the change?

assets.caption:
A customer follows a task across the company. They notice when the explanation changes, when they have to repeat information and when nobody owns the unresolved question.

This review follows a hypothetical reporting customer through marketing, signup, product and support. It separates a missing message from a conflicting rule or a lost handoff. Those are different pieces of work, even if the complaint sounds similar.

I'd run the review with the people who own those moments and give one person responsibility for checking the complete path afterward.

assets.title: Give the claim a visible product counterpart
assets.subtitle: A review card for promise, proof, contradiction and ownership.

slides.title: Review one moment where the claim should hold.
body: Hypothetical claim: stay in control of your subscription. Inspect the actual change or cancellation task.

rows: What control did the customer expect?
Can they inspect the plan, cost and effective date?
Does a hidden rule block the expected change?
Who will change the experience, explain the rule or revise the claim?

annotations.label: Useful evidence
annotations.detail: Record what the person expects before the action, then compare it with what the product does.

assets.caption:
Product and brand decisions meet at the moment the customer checks a promise. If the claim is 'stay in control', changing a subscription should reveal which control the product actually gives them.

This card keeps the claim, the visible proof and the contradicting moment together. A hidden rule may need a product decision. A deliberate restriction may need a clearer explanation. An overstated claim may need to change.

Start with one task you can inspect. That gives the review an owner and a practical decision instead of a broad discussion about whether the brand feels right.
